comments.text: I think both NVIDIA and AMD looked at their profit margins at low-end hardware, then decided it too slim compared to their high-end cards. So, NVIDIA started looking for cheaper ways to gain the performance increase they were looking for over last generation. That switch to relying heavily on L2 cache to make-up for the expensive VRAM and smaller buffer backfired as their calculations were incorrect. Once they realized they made a mistake in their focus, they switched to marketing energy-savings and DLSS 3, which is the last selling point of their marketing. Their 28% current net profit margin being reported on the stock exchange is INSANE! I'm convinced both AMD and Nvidia are being careful about not innovating too much or too quickly so that their net profit margins aren't negatively affected. After COVID, their stocks BLEW UP, now they are slaves to their shareholders.
comments.author: @BtappinHD

comments.text: @BtappinHD  I would only change "After Covid" to mining/Covid. Either one would have been the profit volcano event. Combined... well, that's what is driving this insanity to maintain abnormally high margins on everything.

comments.text:
I don't think you are being fair with the 4060. If you factor in the power consumptions saving vs the 3060, the 4060 is a better buy for sure. Using nvidia figure you can easily save $30 in 4 years playing game for 10 hour/week in the US which is pretty light btw. So the cost per frame should be less than the 3060 and even 3060 ti. That doesn't account for frame gen which can improve the FPS GREATLY with small input lag that 99% of us will not even notice (and frame gen is still improving). If you are in the market right now and decide which NVIDIA you want, the 4060 is the best choice in term of value not the 3060 or 3060 ti.
I agree 15% performance increase is bad compared to last gen which was there 3 years ago and I think NVIDIA is being greedy but that doesn't mean the 4060 is bad. Objectively, it is the best one by far to buy right now in terms of cost per frame.

comments.text:
It's a fair review, but a little harsh because you're only taking one side of the market into consideration. 

I think it depends vastly on how you game and what you value. I think mainstream and Youtube/enthusiasts are on diverging paths, and it'll just grow to be wider in the generations to come, and Nvidia is being forced to pursue one market or the other at the lower end entries to the market.

Mainstream gamers by and large like the razzle dazzle of RT when available and are happy to trade a marginal quality difference for a massive FPS uplift, and will utilize all of the features turned off in these benchmarks. Why? Because they are savy enough to turn them on? Sure, some of them will, but mostly no because they come on by default if the card can support them in any modern title. They are how the games are intended by the developers to be played. I haven't seen a modern title that comes native out of the box in a very long time. It's not intended to push these demanding games at native resolutions with no RT/no upscaling/no frame gen (when available). If it was? You'd have to turn on all those things, not turn them *off*. So the numbers they will see will never be close to what these benchmarks provide. It's literally an apples and oranges gaming experience. For that crowd? This card is just fine, because it'll blow away every AMD/Intel equivalent offered up when you turn all those features on, or even just some of them especially at the resolutions they will be playing at. Which will be 1080p for the majority, or 1440p for the high end among them.
   (Edit: I'll retract that 1440p, in the case of this card? The high end among them aren't using a 60 series card. Period)

YT/Enthusiasts generally only place value on pure native raster at high resolutions and settings, and devalue RT performance, upscaling, and things like frame generation. They don't even feature in most benchmarks. So for that crowd, this card is trash at any price point. It just doesn't meet those performance needs. Even at that $200 point you clarified it's still not a great buy because it's rasterization performance at the higher resolutions "demanded" by YT/Enthusiasts, doesn't work. What was it GN said? 1080p in 2023? It was a laughing point. We'll ignore that the majority of gamers are still gaming at 1080p, which is a fact all three major manufacturers openly acknowledge, much to the chagrin of monitor manufacturers :P

So it comes down to which market do they pursue? You can't make both happy. AMD has shown if you aim for pure rasterization, well you pay the price in power efficiency, RT performance, and upscaling and the all around feature set of the video card. You have to make a decision if you're Nvidia, which do you chase? At the higher end they try to appease both groups, but at the lower end? They do what any public company should do, they pick the larger audience. YT/Enthusiasts represent maybe 2-3 million potential customers, if we're being generous and assume no overlap in viewing, while you have over a 100 million potential customers in the mainstream market. Will they all buy every generation? Of course not, most won't even buy every five to six years or longer, but it's the larger market by far, so you pursue it.

So I think the difference in values will only grow larger in the years to come. As frame generation becomes more and more the standard just as upscaling and RT already have and YT continues to devalue those features? It'll just become a larger and larger divergence of paths and resulting expectations and needs.

To answer those arguing RTX4060 is "mid-range" when its 8GB VRAM is so limiting: 1080p even at ultra settings is NOT midrange in 2023! There are plenty of people who're playing at 4K ULTRA now (high end), so "mid-range" now would be 1440p ULTRA settings with playable FPS and no glitches! Logically this means that basic entry level (budget) gaming in 2023 STARTS at 1080p ULTRA settings with smooth FPS and zero glitches - a 8GB VRAM graphics card CANNOT manage that even with all CURRENT games, with upcoming games planning on needing even more VRAM!

An 8GB VRAM GPU in 2023 is a 720p card, which is a resolution and performance which was long in the tooth a decade ago and should be dead and buried before now!

Another point: low VRAM requires MUCH bigger game installations (150GB not unusual) because it has to include crappy low resolution textures, as well as photorealistic textures for those with enough VRAM, to allow MIPMAPPING, which increases used drive space by a huge 33%! Aim for a GPU with 16GB VRAM or more, even if that means switching to AMD as high VRAM graphics makes a MUCH bigger difference the fake extra filler frames that cause latency by NVidia!

comments.text:
I think a rough approximation for us prices is, for every 10 watts running 10 hours a day, at 15 cents a US kwh, or 35 cents a European kwh, would cost about 5$ a year (us), or 12$ a year (europe) per 10 watt increment at 10 hr/day heavy use.

For say, performance per watt, the 1080 will use max at 170-220 watts. The 4060 at 115 watts, will be a savings of about 50-100 watts. At 10 hrs a day heavy gaming maxing out the watts, (heavily generous situation), this would be a cost of 25$-60$ a year in electricity over the 1080. 

Assuming a best case scenario (say, selling the 1080 11 gb for 150$, spending 300$ to get the 4060), you would need near 3-6 years at extremely heavy (10 hr/day gaming, 24/7, 365/365 days a year) to break even after several years. 

Thing is, you can preview your computer energy use, and you often don't run at max. (Or can underclock when you're happy with 60-75 fps), with the nvidia alt z panel, and my 3060ti underclocked (70% performance for 44% electricity, 160% power efficiency, and silent fans/no heat), really averages like 10-15 watts idling, 20-30 watts playing l4d2 at ultra, 40-60 watts playing ow2 at low vs ultra settings.

I only ever really hit the wattage limit pushing the system and overclocking to 220W on ai tasks like Stable diffusion or maxing Rdr2.

Even then, the rates to break even are LITERALLY near 24/7, 365/365 day rates. If one does web browsing you barely consume 15 watts. You have to constantly have your pc stressed to the point the case feels like a 70-80C + heat bomb. Even then, if heat is really a concern, underclocking takes the 3-6 years to literal 6-12 year times to break even.. 

And gpus tend to double in performance for the previous cost every 5-7 years. 

Cliffnotes:
o If you used the 4060 for 10 hours of heavy, 100% gaming a day. It'd take 3-6 years under optimal 24/7 365/365 rates to break even.|
o If electricity costs/ heat were a primary concern, undervolting for 70% performance for 44% power usage doubles that time to 6-13 years to break even
o You have to game for 3600 hours a year to break even in 3-6 years.. If you play 500 hrs a year, the time literally becomes 21-35 years...

o If you run ai/stable diffusion or bitcoin mined however, 24/7 365 usage could indeed pay itself back. So 4000s for a ai hosting company or 24/7 generations might make sense. 
o For home users, the more you game 2000-4000+ hours a year, the more important energy savings are. The less you do, (100-1000 hr/year), The more marginal they may be. 
o Gpus tend to double in performance every 5-7 years. By the time you'd have broken even on generous power use.. The gpu might be obsolete.

comments.text:
Yeah dlss can double the frame rate, however at 1/10th speed, dlss can add input latency, and often gets the frames by 'smearing' them instead of drawing unique frames. It looks fine in motion but it majorly reduces camera quality turning, and you lose the crispness of frame to frame images.

It depends what you want. If one wants fps for the smoothness it adds competitive gaming, the input delay on a game like ow2 doesn't even have dlss/dlss 3.

It will add input delays. You get the frames but they're literally just smeared frames. It's a lot like animation interpolation. It looks great when standing still looking at a flat screen, but the screen can blur every time you turn a camera, taking still pictures of interpolated frames will reveal smeared cars with their headlights missing. It feels like it defeats the point to run at ultra and have smeared frames missing core details vs just tweaking settings down a little and having 60-120 real frames per second, vs 30 slightly better ultra ones, with 90 fake ones inserted. 

The whole point of fps for first person shooters is to make aiming better, the game more responsive. Dlss is a technology that looks great on camera or for youtube where it's cropped anyways and it looks alright in motion. But it's still a lot of camera tricks. The fps aren't true frames and they're a lot more like camera smears with input delay that run counterintuitive to the reason you get fps. (Smoothness, visual clarity, responsiveness of the frames, VS sacrificing all of those FOR the frames.) 

It's not a bad technology, if you don't mind input lag it's okay, but a lot of the images it generates are not true 100% quality, but image smears that look fine in motion but horrible when paused. And because the frames aren't always real, you add input delay to frames that can't react to your immediate actions either. It's like gaming at the "fluidity" of 30 fps while the 120 fps on screen is a illusion added in after effects.

comments.text:
I really don't get Nvidia's "cache makes less VRAM bandwidth okay!" position... to me it makes no sense.

VRAM exists because GPUs need things faster than they can be streamed from system memory, or system storage.

The only way for cache to make up for a VRAM deficiency is to bypass it entirely and load things directly to cache from system memory or system storage. Otherwise, what you're saying is "our gains from more cache is more than our losses from crap memory configuration!"... and that only works when your crap memory configuration is, in fact, more than you needed anyway. If you look at anybody's frame-time charts, you can tell pretty quickly that, in this case, it's not enough.

And also, let us be thankful that Samsung/Micron/SK Hynix can't make 32Gb (4GB) GDDR6 chips, or we would be getting sold 64-bit memory buses instead of 128-bit.

But i'm not paying $399 for a mass produced low cost 50 class card, and adding $20 worth of RAM, is not going to convice me to shell out $500 for 50 class performance.
And before an Nvidia share-holder tries to tell me the 4060TI is a 60 class, just stop, i'm not an idiot, dont piss on my head and tell me its raining. If you keep pushing me, i have a more valid argument than yours, that this is actually a 30 class card, its not, but the argument is more accurate than "oh its faster than last gen so it must be a higher tier"
Yea buddy, thats why they get a new name every year, and we're calling this an Ada RTX 4060, not calling this a Kepler GTX 499.9999, the generation lets you know the architecture is faster, the last 2 numbers indicate the product stack, the actual class of card is dictated by the die size and memory bus.

If it helps just dis-ascociate the branding of GTX/RTX from the class, calling it "50 class" is just much faster than saying it is "100-200mm 128 bit class"


Regardless of performance, the 120-200mm class dies are 50 class, they generally have 128 bit bus but they can have more and IIRC there was a 96 bit out there somewhere by AMD.
200-300mm are 60 class with 192-256 bit bus, these can be cut down and have a narrower bus to be turned into a 50 branded card, but the 3050, is just a cut down 60 class card, also the 1070/1080 were 60 class
300-400mm are 70 class cards, like the GTX 970, RTX 3070, and RTX 4080 generally have a 256 bit bus(can be cut down to 192 to be turned into a 60 branded card like the RTX 2060, and RTX 3060TI, this saves money over producing a new die just for those cards)
400-500mm are 80 class, like the GTX 780TI, GTX 1080TI/Titan, RTX 2070/2080/2060KO, (absent for 4000 series)
500-800mm are 80TI/90/Titan class, like the 980TI, Pascal GP100(no gaming cards were made this generation because AMD's best could only compete with the 60 class card, so they shifted all the names up, sort of like they're doing with the 40 series), 2080TI, 3080 through 3090TI, and 4090 generally have a 385-512 bit bus, can be cut down to 256 bit bus to make 80 or even 70 branded cards

You can put a little more nuance in there, like take Pascal for instance, you could argue that a 60 class card is 1/2 the die size and memory bus of the top card, and the price must be 1/3rd to 1/4th that of the flagship, but that should put the 4070TI at between $399, and $539 as a 4060, and the 4060 should be called a 4050 and priced aroudn $119 which is too low, but this is because the 4090 is priced lower than expected, it is on a ~60% more expensive node, basically the same size as the 3090, so that should price the 4090 at $2400 MSRP

Oh, almost forgot about the 30 class, they're 0-120mm with 32-96 bit bus, these generally are designed featureless, lacking things like video encoders, but more often than not XX30, are really just 50 class cards cut down to a narrower bus with features and cores dissabled becuase the 50 class is already so small, they're not saving much money by tooling and masking out a smaller die. If there were more demand for 30 class cards they would, but at the volume these cards sell it is cheaper to take a 50 class and disable parts of it, than to design and build and entire production process.

comments.text:
I've said it before, and I'll say it again. Seems like, to Nvidia, the ONLY reason to continue pushing with the whole 40 series is the pretext of DLSS 3 and Frame Generation.

Yes, upscaling tech can make the difference between unplayable and "playable with slight compromises" (whether visual or latency related), and it's nice to have them around and I wish for the tech to mature and improve over time. BUT, upscaling tech shouldn't have to be the main reason to sell the product, while neglecting the generational uplift and raw rasterization power... Aside from the 4090, which is (in my opinion) the most ridiculous generational jump I've seen in a while. And a lot of people, myself included, were hoping for the whole Ada Lovelace lineup to follow suit, but seems like the lower you go down the chain, the worse it gets, it's like they're not even trying anymore. 

Technically speaking, they're not even selling a "1080p" card. They're selling a 720p card (quality) or a 626p card (balanced), if their main selling point is DLSS 3. Also half the framerate if we're counting Frame Generation (since the tensor cores are working on every other frame to create a new image).

It only makes the 3060 12GB, 6650XT, 6700, and 6700XT, look like a better investment option, even if it's for 2-4 more years. Hell, even the 7600 looks more reasonable at $270 (actually on sale for $260, was $250 last week).

comments.text: Don't forget to up your minimum clock speed for your 6700XT. I've nearly gone mad trying to figure out why my 6700XT fluctuate so much in terms of FPS. Turns out the clock speed is all over the place. In some situations when not much power is required, the card runs at 1000-1200 mhz and will suddenly ramp up to 2500 mhz when it is required to do so. That much spike causes the gameplay to stutter a lot. So now I set the minimum clock speed to 1900 mhz and that fixes the issue and now games run smooth like butter. AMD cards are good but it's definitely not newbie friendly, requires a lot of tuning and that's probably why Nvidia still holds the majority of the market in their hands.

Mmmm... gimme that juicy 146 mm2 die, which you can store 486 times in a single TSMC 5nm wafer which apparently costs around 15K USD. Even if you consider the fact, that the yield from a single wafer is atrocious 70% (which is not, it's more like 90+%), from a single purchased wafer by NVIDIA, the company makes 338 RTX 4060 dies ready to go. 338 RTX-es 4060 is 101 000 USD. Even if you take 70%, very small yields and account for a cost not only the GPU but also graphics card PCB and components, it still puts NVIDIA at around 50k USD of pure profit. Let that sink in.

Now. The average yield of 5nm TSMC wafer is apparently at 80%, approaching over 90% for a very small dies (18mm2). If you take 85% lets say (to account for the RTX 4060 being so small and RTX 4090 being so large (large = less yield)), NVIDIA makes 413 working RTX 4060 GPU from a single wafer. 413 GPU's means 123K USD. Minus the graphics card components, logistics and all of that, It gives them more like 70-80K USD of pure profit.

comments.text:
Yeah i think i did a look. If nvidia had held up to their past generations of offering each gen a tier above, with pricing to match. The 4060/ti would have been a 20% better card (exceeding the 3070), available for 30% less price, (220-300$ vs 300-400$). Resulting in about 50% more frames per buck. 

Instead, the 4060 is often a poorer value than last gen with less vram for a 300-400$ 8 gb 4060/ti, while the 12 gb 3060 occassionaly comes at 200-250$ used, and the 20-30% higher fps 8 gb 3060ti.

Dlss does raise framerates, but taken in 1/10 slow mo, the pictures are often blurry, low quality and artifacted image like 60 fps interpolation. They look fine in motion. But people calling them "fake framerates" aren't exactly wrong either. You're paying a 100-200$ price for a card to run on ultra only to have all your high end textures smeared and it seems to add a input delay, make swift camera movement look worse, moving textures like shining cracks on pavement crisp at lower settings get blurred away. 

Dlss still sounds like a good technology for 4k upscaling on a budget. But it seems a paradox to go for high end textures in the first place over going medium settings for crisp visual quality, vs detailed but BLURRY with doubled input delay, less movement clarity. It feels like the definition of frames over gameplay. it looks great for a tech demo where you don't face input delay and youtube compresses the video anyways. 

But i'd prefer to have crisp frames running at medium 120 fps settings, rather than run 30 real frames and 120 "real" fake frames that use ultra settings only to blur over them. 

Im not trying to be a graphics head either, just legit for rdr2 with dlss on vs off, my card had wonderful shadows, crisp textures, and the difference in dlss comes with a frame hit for 1080p while making movement blurry and looking worse at native. It sounds like a good 4k tech, but it just doesn't make a lot of sense. 

Still nvidia is entitled to their stockholders, selling consumers a 4x better gpu, while cutting their 50% profit margins isn't exactly evil.. But they could put 32 gb of vram on a graphics card for 110$ at 27$ per 8 gb vram apparently.. And released a 11 gb vram card... 7 years ago on the 1080. 

Clearly they have the capacity to make a higher vram quanity than 8 gb on 700$ cards in 2023 with ram prices 2-4x lower than they have ever been. 

But it feels like intentionally planned obsolence.. They want to sell us a 700$ 8 gb card we need to buy twice, with 50% margins to make 350$ twice. 
VS: Rather than a 500$ 32 gb vram, same performance price, with a 100-200$ cut, and sell once. 350$ profit sold twice is clearly more profit than 100-200$.. But man does it suck to be the consumer getting milked and bilked by a company into buying expiring garbage while it'll eventually produce more eventual electronic waste..

@Notyouraveragename while it's possible nvidia had crypto mining in mind when they were designing the 40 series, the improved efficiency vs. the 30 series isn't very strong evidence for that claim.

The efficiency improvements are probably mostly due to being manufactured on a smaller process (TSMC 4N vs the 30 series' Samsung 8LPP process).

Having "longer laptop battery life" (or gaming handhelds) is enough of a selling point to move to the newer process.

In fairness to nvidia's engineers, the efficiency improvements aren't just because of the new process. In addition to architectural changes they've done to the cores, the 4060 has 24 MB of L2 cache, a pretty huge increase over the 3060's 3 MB (for the 12GB model, the 8GB 3060 had just 2 MB).

It's a shame nvidia decided to hamper their low-end 40 series cards in other ways. :-/
